p.src: The two-state spin remains our simplest quantum system. A three-state Hilbert space would be the next simplest abstract possibility; two spins already have four orthogonal basis states. We will not yet compose two spins, although that step is close and will bring entanglement with it. First we should finish the one-spin problem and put the ideas of uncertainty and time evolution on firmer ground.

u.src: When Two Quantities Can Be Definite Together

p.src: A good measurement is repeatable. If an observable is measured and the value $l$ is obtained, an immediate repetition should return the same value. The first measurement must therefore leave the system, at least momentarily, in an eigenstate of the corresponding operator: $L\ket{l}=l\ket{l}.$ This operational statement is enough to expose the qualitative origin of uncertainty.

p.src:
Suppose two observables $L$ and $M$ can be measured simultaneously. A joint measurement must leave both reported values definite. Its possible post-measurement states must consequently be simultaneous eigenvectors of both operators. In the finite-dimensional setting used here, we may choose a complete orthonormal set $\{\ket{i}\}$ satisfying $L\ket{i}=l_i\ket{i},
\qquad
M\ket{i}=m_i\ket{i}.$

p.src: The converse is also true: commuting Hermitian operators can be simultaneously diagonalized. If one operator has a degenerate eigenspace, the other preserves that eigenspace, and it can be diagonalized within it. Repeating this in every eigenspace produces a complete common eigenbasis.

p.src: The Pauli operators give the first important counterexample. No two of $\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z$ commute. The eigenstates of $\sigma_z$ are up and down, while those of $\sigma_x$ are right and left. One may prepare either component sharply and repeat its measurement, but one cannot prepare both components sharply at once. This is uncertainty before any numerical inequality has been introduced.

p.src: Unitary Evolution and Its Generator

u.src: Unitary Evolution and Its Generator
en: Unitary Evolution and Its Generator

p.src: Quantum mechanics took considerably longer than classical mechanics to define a state, but once the state space is established the rule for motion is compact. Let $\ket{\psi(t)}=U(t)\ket{\psi(0)}.$ Time evolution must preserve distinguishability. More strongly, it preserves all inner products. For an orthonormal basis, $\bra{j}U^\dagger(t)U(t)\ket{i}=\delta_{ji},$ and therefore $U^\dagger(t)U(t)=I.$ The evolution operator is unitary.

For an orthonormal basis, $\bra{j}U^\dagger(t)U(t)\ket{i}=\delta_{ji},$ and therefore $U^\dagger(t)U(t)=I.$ The evolution operator is unitary.

For an orthonormal basis, $\bra{j}U^\dagger(t)U(t)\ket{i}=\delta_{ji},$ and therefore $U^\dagger(t)U(t)=I.$ The evolution operator is unitary.

p.src:
At zero elapsed time $U(0)=I$. Continuity then says that evolution through a small time $\epsilon$ differs only slightly from the identity. In units with $\hbar=1$, write $U(\epsilon)=I-i\epsilon H+O(\epsilon^2),
\qquad
U^\dagger(\epsilon)=I+i\epsilon H^\dagger+O(\epsilon^2).$ Substitution into Equation  gives $H^\dagger=H.$ The generator of time evolution is Hermitian and is therefore an observable. It is the Hamiltonian.

p.src: Schrödinger’s original equation concerned the wavefunction of a moving particle. The operator statement above was once called the generalized Schrödinger equation because it applies equally to a spin, a three-state system, two spins, or a system of arbitrary complexity. p.src: Equation  gives a definite evolution of the state when the system is left undisturbed. This does not make every experimental outcome definite. A quantum state determines probabilities for possible measurements, and the equation updates those probabilities through the changing amplitudes. Measurement generally changes the state and interrupts this isolated evolution.

p.src: Because $H$ is Hermitian, its eigenvalues are real and its eigenvectors can be chosen as a complete orthonormal basis: $H\ket{E_i}=E_i\ket{E_i}.$ This is the time-independent form of the Schrödinger equation. It is an eigenvalue problem rather than an equation of motion: it asks which energy values the system can have and which states have those values sharply.

p.src: The spectrum depends on the system. Bound atomic motion and the harmonic oscillator have countable energy levels. An unbound particle may have a continuous spectrum. Energy can be measured in many ways; in principle even a sufficiently precise mass measurement could use $E=mc^2$, although that is rarely the practical method. A real system already has its Hamiltonian; the physicist does not dictate it but tries to discover it. Once that operator is known, finding its eigenvalues and eigenvectors is the mathematical task.

p.src: The Algebra of Commutators

u.src: The Algebra of Commutators
en: The Algebra of Commutators

p.src:
Commutators are antisymmetric: $=-[B,A].$ They also obey a product rule analogous to the Leibniz rule for derivatives: $=A[B,C]+[A,C]B.$ To verify it, preserve the order of every factor: $\begin{aligned}
A[B,C]+[A,C]B
&=A(BC-CB)\\
&\quad +(AC-CA)B\\
&=ABC-ACB\\
&\quad +ACB-CAB\\
&=ABC-CAB\\
&=[AB,C].\end{aligned}$

p.src:
The same antisymmetry and product rule hold for classical Poisson brackets. This structural resemblance is not accidental. The classical correspondence is $\{A,B\}
\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{1}{i\hbar}[A,B]
=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[A,B].$ In $\hbar=1$ units, the classical equation $\frac{dL}{dt}=\{L,H\}$ has the same form as Equation . In ordinary macroscopic units $\hbar$ is tiny, and commutators become negligible in the appropriate classical limit. This is the essential check that identifies the quantum generator $H$ with the Hamiltonian of classical mechanics.

=-i\expect{[H,H]}=0.$ For the time-independent Hamiltonians under discussion, the average energy is conserved. A stronger statement about the full energy distribution is possible, but the average is all that is needed here.

Thus the general solution is $\ket{\psi(t)}

p.src: A Spin in a Magnetic Field

u.src: A Spin in a Magnetic Field
en: A Spin in a Magnetic Field

p.src: What Hamiltonian should be assigned to one spin? An isolated spin in otherwise empty space has no nontrivial preferred direction, so its Hamiltonian is proportional to the identity and produces no observable motion. A magnetic field supplies both an interaction energy and an axis.

p.src: Take the field along $z$. A charged particle with spin carries a magnetic moment, and the familiar dipole energy is proportional to the alignment of that moment with the field. Absorb the field strength, magnetic moment, sign convention, and $\hbar$ into one constant $\omega$: $H=\frac{\omega}{2}\sigma_z.$ The factor of $1/2$ is convenient because Pauli commutators contain a factor of $2$.

p.src:
The first two equations describe circular motion in the transverse plane: $\begin{aligned}
\expect{\sigma_x}(t)
&=\expect{\sigma_x}(0)\cos\omega t
-\expect{\sigma_y}(0)\sin\omega t,\\
\expect{\sigma_y}(t)
&=\expect{\sigma_x}(0)\sin\omega t
+\expect{\sigma_y}(0)\cos\omega t.\end{aligned}$ Meanwhile $\expect{\sigma_z}$ is constant. The expectation-value vector therefore precesses around the magnetic-field axis with angular frequency $\omega$.

u.src:
The first two equations describe circular motion in the transverse plane: $\begin{aligned}
\expect{\sigma_x}(t)
&=\expect{\sigma_x}(0)\cos\omega t
-\expect{\sigma_y}(0)\sin\omega t,\\
\expect{\sigma_y}(t)
&=\expect{\sigma_x}(0)\sin\omega t
+\expect{\sigma_y}(0)\cos\omega t.\end{aligned}$ Meanwhile $\expect{\sigma_z}$ is constant. The expectation-value vector therefore precesses around the magnetic-field axis with angular frequency $\omega$.

p.src: The Most General One-Spin Hamiltonian

u.src: The Most General One-Spin Hamiltonian
en: The Most General One-Spin Hamiltonian

p.src:
Every Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix can be expanded as $H=aI+b_x\sigma_x+b_y\sigma_y+b_z\sigma_z,$ with real coefficients. The identity term changes only the overall phase. The three remaining coefficients can be regarded as the components of a vector. Writing their magnitude as $\omega/2$ and their direction as a unit vector $\bm n$, the nontrivial Hamiltonian becomes $H=\frac{\omega}{2}\,\bm\sigma\cdot\bm n,
\qquad
\bm\sigma\cdot\bm n
=n_x\sigma_x+n_y\sigma_y+n_z\sigma_z.$ If $\bm B=B\bm n$, then $\bm n$ carries the direction of the field while $\omega$ carries its magnitude together with the magnetic coupling. It is $\bm n$, not $\omega$, that records orientation.

=\omega\,\bm n\times\expect{\bm\sigma}.$ The component along $\bm n$ commutes with $H$ and remains fixed; the perpendicular components precess around $\bm n$.

p.src: The Two Energy Levels

u.src: The Two Energy Levels
en: The Two Energy Levels

p.src:
Writing Equation  as a matrix gives $\bm\sigma\cdot\bm n
=
\begin{pmatrix}
n_z & n_x-in_y\\
n_x+in_y & -n_z
\end{pmatrix}.$ Let its eigenvalues be $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$. Its trace is zero: $\lambda_1+\lambda_2=0.$ For a unit vector $n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2=1$, its determinant is $\begin{aligned}
\lambda_1\lambda_2
&=\det(\bm\sigma\cdot\bm n)\\
&=-n_z^2-(n_x-in_y)(n_x+in_y)\\
&=-(n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2)\\
&=-1.\end{aligned}$ The two eigenvalues are therefore $\lambda_\pm=\pm1.$

p.src: We have now exhausted the nontrivial time-independent dynamics of a single spin. The same algebra that first signaled uncertainty also generates its motion: noncommuting Pauli matrices turn the Hamiltonian into precession, while the component commuting with the Hamiltonian remains conserved. The next increase in complexity is not another one-spin Hamiltonian but a larger state space, where independent systems can be composed and entangled.
